# WHAT IS IN THE TANKS IN B RING [color=#5E7066]Pinned. Describe what you saw, how close you were, and how long you looked.[/color]
### #1 pump_tech_rho (OP) // 83.04.11 I service the circulation pumps on a row of tanks in a sealed ring at a research site. I do not go inside the room. The pumps are on the far side of a wall and I see the tanks through a service window about the size of a ration tray, at an angle, while I swap filters.
Twelve tanks, floor to ceiling, glass gone milky at the edges. The fluid is amber, like weak tea. It is kept warm, which is why the pumps cook every few months. Most of the tanks look empty, or I think they do, the fluid is too cloudy to see the back.
Tank seven is not empty. Last cycle, while I was on my knees with a filter in my hand, something in tank seven turned over. Slowly, the way you roll over in bed. I saw a hand. It had the right number of fingers. They were too long.
### #2 floor_polish // 83.04.11 Custodial, different ring, same kind of room. I clean the floor in front of the tanks once a week with a supervisor watching me. You are not supposed to look up, so I look at the floor, and the floor is how I know there is something in them.
The glass sweats a little, all the time, and the drips on the floor around tanks four and nine have a dull ring to them in the morning, like the polish was eaten. Nothing else in that room does that. Not the coolant, not the cleaner. I have tested.
### #3 just_a_pig // 83.04.12 Respectfully, people. Medical schools keep animal specimens in preservative. Fetal pigs, primate arms, whatever. A long fingered hand in a tank in a lab is the least surprising thing I have ever heard.
### #4 pump_tech_rho (OP) // 83.04.12 You do not heat a preservative. You do not run a pump on it day and night with a nutrient feed line going in at the top. I know because I am the one who changes the feed line.
And dead pigs do not roll over.
### #5 lab_glass_wash // 83.04.14 I wash glassware in the specimen wing. Not the big tanks. Jars. Shelves of them, each with a number and a date and nothing else on the label.
Most are tissue. Grey slices. Some are whole. There is a row of eight big jars that are always cleaned last and always by me, because the others will not. Each one holds the same thing. The best I can describe it is a hand, a pale one, about the size of a dinner plate, the fingers folded under it like a spider sitting on a stone, and a long tail wrapped around underneath. Some jars have one. Jar three has two, wrapped around each other.
The date on jar three is newer than the others. Somebody is still collecting them.
### #6 shift_guard_ii // 83.04.15 You are describing the same thing the survey crew brought back to our site in a cold case. I was on the dock. The case was marked rock sample. A rock does not come with a scientist walking beside it holding the handle like it is her child.
### #7 duty_cycle (mod) // 83.04.15 Reminder for new readers. Nothing in this thread has been seen up close by anyone qualified to say what it is. That includes the people posting it. Read it as accounts, not answers. The closest thing to a biologist who has written about the jars is at [netlink="fieldnotes.deep" link="fieldnotes.deep"], and that is one person's notebook.
### #8 floor_polish // 83.04.22 The supervisor caught me looking up today. She did not shout. She said, very quietly, that the glass on four had been scratched on the inside overnight and to tell her if I saw any more scratches, and then to leave the room and not finish the floor.
Scratched on the inside.
### #9 pump_tech_rho (OP) // 83.04.30 Tank seven was drained this week. I know because the pump for seven was switched off at the panel and tagged with a work order I did not write. The work order says [italic]subject transferred to sublevel three, tank decommissioned.[/italic]
A tank does not get a subject. A subject is a person.
